rules.quote: Structure the parts of a sentence so meaning is easy to understand.
rules.specification: The page gives no operational threshold for ‘easy to understand’. The boundary between acceptable structural complexity and unclear sentence structure needs reviewer judgement.
rules.violation_condition: The arrangement of a sentence’s parts obscures its meaning or makes the relationships between those parts difficult to understand.
rules.why: G-5: this instruction concerns an observable property of the text—structural clarity—rather than a writer-side checking action.

covers.quote: You could also write this as 2 short sentences, but this approach can appear repetitive.

parts.quote: The agency planned to start the project next year but ran out of funding.

examples.note: The manual permits this alternative; it does not present it as incorrect.

parts.quote: The agency planned to start the project next year. The agency ran out of funding.

rules.quote: If the 2 clauses share the same subject, don’t repeat the subject
rules.violation_condition: The subject is explicitly repeated in the second of two coordinated clauses that share a subject.
when: The two clauses are coordinated within one sentence and share a subject.
Repeating the subject in two separate sentences is permitted.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: retain the shared-subject condition and the separate-sentences permission; G-6: the comma instruction belongs to the principal-clause rule on commas.md.

covers.quote: Build most sentences in this order with active voice when using active verbs (doing or action verbs).

parts.quote: Computer models produce wind forecasts to show average speeds.

examples.note: The manual presents this as an example of justified passive voice.

parts.quote: A formal complaint was made about the use of discriminatory language.

rules.quote: Use passive voice only if there is a good reason – for example, if you can’t say who did the action or because information has to be concealed for ethical or legal reasons.
rules.specification: The active-voice instruction and the restriction on passive voice form one check. ‘A good reason’ is not defined exhaustively and requires contextual judgement; ‘most sentences’ does not supply a numerical quota.
rules.violation_condition: An action verb is used in passive voice without a good reason for choosing passive rather than active voice.
when: The verb expresses doing or action.
Passive voice is permitted when there is a good reason.
Examples of good reasons include being unable to say who did the action and needing to conceal information for ethical or legal reasons.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the active-voice preference and passive-voice restriction into one check, with the stated reasons retained as exceptions.
